title: Doing many things at once
summary: ForEach-Object -Parallel with -ThrottleLimit and $using:, thread jobs, why shared variables do not work across threads, and how to stay polite to the systems you call.

steps.title: ForEach-Object -Parallel
body: Checking 200 servers one after another, at 1 second each, takes over three minutes. Most of that time is
**waiting** (for the network, a disk, an API), so doing several at once is almost free:
```powershell
$timeout = 5
Get-Content ./servers.txt | ForEach-Object -Parallel {
$ok = Test-Connection $_ -Count 1 -TimeoutSeconds $using:timeout -Quiet
[pscustomobject]@{ Server = $_; Up = $ok }
} -ThrottleLimit 10 | Sort-Object Server
- Each item runs in its **own runspace** (a separate PowerShell inside the same process, on its own thread).
PowerShell 7 only; Windows PowerShell 5.1 has no `-Parallel`.
- **`-ThrottleLimit`** (default **5**) is how many run at once. Pick it for the *other side*: a small API may answer
`429 Too Many Requests` or fall over at 50 parallel calls.
- Variables from outside are **not** visible inside: use **`$using:name`** to pass a copy in.
- Results come back in **completion order**, not input order: sort them if order matters.
**Thread jobs** run a script block in the background while your script carries on:
```powershell
$job = Start-ThreadJob { Invoke-RestMethod https://reports.example.com/build -TimeoutSec 300 }
# ... other work ...
$report = Receive-Job $job -Wait -AutoRemoveJob
`Start-ThreadJob` ships with PowerShell 7 (since 7.6 its module is called `Microsoft.PowerShell.ThreadJob`) and is much lighter
than the old `Start-Job`, which starts a whole new process per job.

steps.prompt: Inside `ForEach-Object -Parallel { ... }`, you need the value of `$cutoff` that the script set earlier. How?
steps.explain: Each parallel block runs in a fresh runspace with none of your variables. `$using:` copies the value in. It is read-only in spirit: assigning to it is a parse error, and changes to the copy never come back.

steps.title: Twelve slow endpoints in a few seconds
prompt: `~/scripts/endpoints.txt` lists 12 endpoints of the lesson API; each takes **1 second** to answer `{"id": ..., "ok": true}`.
The API allows **at most 8** concurrent calls (more get `429`).
Write `~/scripts/check-endpoints.ps1` that calls them all **in parallel** (with a sensible `-ThrottleLimit`) and
prints one line per endpoint, **`<id> ok`** (or `<id> failed`), **sorted by id**. The whole script must finish in
under 6 seconds (one by one would take 12).

checks.name: twelve ok lines, sorted
checks.expectOutput: svc01 ok svc02 ok svc03 ok svc04 ok svc05 ok svc06 ok svc07 ok svc08 ok svc09 ok svc10 ok svc11 ok svc12 ok
checks.fail: The script should print `svc01 ok` to `svc12 ok`, one per line, in order. A `failed` line usually means too many calls at once (429).

checks.name: finishes in under 6 seconds
checks.cmd: s=$(date +%s%N); timeout 20 pwsh -NoProfile -NonInteractive -File ~/scripts/check-endpoints.ps1 >/dev/null 2>&1; t=$(( ($(date +%s%N) - s) / 1000000 )); echo "took ${t} ms"; test $t -lt 6000
checks.fail: The run took too long. Use `ForEach-Object -Parallel` with a `-ThrottleLimit` between 4 and 8.

hints: Inside: `try { $r = Invoke-RestMethod $_ -TimeoutSec 5; "$($r.id) ok" } catch { ... "failed" }`. For the id of a failed call, take it from the URL: `($_ -split 'id=')[1]`.
Pipe the results into `Sort-Object` before they are printed.
explain: With 6 at a time, 12 one-second calls take about 2 seconds. The throttle is a promise to the system you call:
a busy production API, a domain controller or a database can be hurt by a laptop running 100 threads. Start low,
measure, raise it only if the other side is fine.

steps.explain: Each block has its own empty `$count` (it does not even see the outer one). Nothing comes back to the caller except **output**. To collect results, output them and gather them outside: `$n = (1..5 | ForEach-Object -Parallel { 1 } | Measure-Object).Count`.

steps.title: total bytes: 0
prompt: `pwsh -File ~/scripts/total-size.ps1` scans each regional share in parallel and always says `total bytes: 0`.
Fix it so it prints the real total of everything under `~/shares` (still scanning the shares in parallel).

checks.name: the real total
checks.cmd: want=$(find ~/shares -type f -printf '%s\n' | awk '{s+=$1} END {print s}'); got=$(pwsh -NoProfile -NonInteractive -File ~/scripts/total-size.ps1 2>&1 | tr -d '\r'); echo "$got (expected total bytes: $want)"; test "$got" = "total bytes: $want"
checks.fail: The script should print `total bytes: <the real sum>`.

checks.name: still parallel
checks.fail: Keep `ForEach-Object -Parallel`: on the real shares, scanning one by one takes an hour.

hints: `$total += $size` inside the block changes a different `$total` in the block's own runspace, which is thrown away.
Make each block **output** its size instead (just `$size` on its own line).
solution: # total-size.ps1: adds up the size of every regional share, one share per thread (the real shares are slow to scan).
explain: The rule for parallel code: **no shared mutable state**. Each worker outputs its result; the caller combines them.
